original_txt: BIND9 - Denial of Service Exploit in the Wild Skip to primary navigation Skip to content Skip to primary sidebar Skip to footer Sucuri Blog Website Security News Products Website Security Platform Website Firewall (WAF) Enterprise Website Security Multisite Solutions Features Detection Protection Performance Response Backups Partners Agency Solutions Partners Referral Program Ecommerce Resources Guides Webinars Infographics SiteCheck Reports Email Courses Immediate Help Login Menu BIND9 \xe2\x80\x93 Denial of Service Exploit in the Wild August 2, 2015Daniel Cid 121 SHARES FacebookTwitterSubscribe BIND is one of the most popular DNS servers in the world. It comes bundled with almost every cPanel, VPS and dedicated server installation and is used by most DNS providers. A week ago, the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) team released a patch for a serious denial of service vulnerability (CVE-2015-5477) that allows a remote and unauthenticated attacker to crash the BIND (named) daemon, taking down a\xc2 DNS server. This\xc2 happens because of an error in\xc2 the way\xc2 BIND handles TKEY queries, which with a single UDP packet can trigger a required assertion failure, causing the DNS daemon to exit. Exploits in the Wild Because of its severity we\xe2\x80\x99ve been actively monitoring to see when the exploit would be live. We can confirm that the attacks have begun. DNS is one of the most critical parts of the Internet infrastructure, so having your DNS go down also means your email, HTTP and all other services will be unavailable. If You Have Not Patched Your DNS Server, Do it Now! All major Linux distributions (Redhat, Centos, Ubuntu, etc) have already provided patches for it and a simple \xe2\x80\x9cyum update\xe2\x80\x9d on Redhat/Centos or \xe2\x80\x9capt-get update\xe2\x80\x9d on Debian-based systems will get you protected. Remember though, for the change to take affect you must restart BIND after the update. If you run your own DNS server, a quick way to see if you are being targeted is to look for the \xe2\x80\x9cANY TKEY\xe2\x80\x9d in your DNS logs: Aug 2 10:32:48 dns named[2717]: client a.b.c.d#42212 (foo.bar): view north_america: query: foo.bar ANY TKEY + (x.y.z.zz) In fact, you can look for any type of TKEY request, as they are not very common, and see if there have been any attempts. The example above is from one of the public exploits released. Note that you need to have querylog enabled (which you can do with the command \xe2\x80\x9crndc querylog on\xe2\x80\x9c). Clients using our DNS server, part of our Website Firewall, are already protected against this vulnerability. For existing customers, you can enable the use of our DNS manager and find instructions in our knowledgebase. 121 SHARES FacebookTwitterSubscribe Categories: Vulnerability Disclosure, Website SecurityTags: DDoS About Daniel Cid Daniel B. Cid is Founder of Sucuri and the VP of Engineering for the GoDaddy Security Products group. He is also the founder of OSSEC and CleanBrowsing. You can find more about Daniel on his site dcid.me or on Twitter: @danielcid Reader Interactions Comments Daniel August 2, 2015 yum update is not enough for centos 6, you need to enable continuous release repo first: https://www.centos.org/forums/viewtopic.php?f=17&t=53532 The AlieN August 5, 2015 I saw this on another site: You can also apply the following patch to your vulnerable version of BIND 9. diff \xe2\x80\x93git a/lib/dns/tkey.c b/lib/dns/tkey.c index 66210d5..34ad90b 100644 \xe2\x80\x94 a/lib/dns/tkey.c +++ b/lib/dns/tkey.c @@ -654,6 +654,7 @@ dns_tkey_processquery(dns_message_t *msg, dns_tkeyctx_t *tctx, * Try the answer section, since that\xe2\x80\x99s where Win2000 * puts it. */ + name = NULL; if (dns_message_findname(msg, DNS_SECTION_ANSWER, qname, dns_rdatatype_tkey, 0, &name, &tkeyset) != ISC_R_SUCCESS) { Can you confirm if the patch can be applied in lieu of the update.
